title: What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans
body: Nature and Environment Europe What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans Jennifer Collins 10/19/2026 October 19, 2026 Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is already harming people. https://p.dw.com/p/5OKVu From tiny bees to big whales, all of the players on nature's team are essential Image: Yonhap News/IMAGO Advertisement From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It's another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job. When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human wellbeing. "It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day," said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF "And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning." Without biodiversity, the variety of food humans eat would not be available. Declining biodiversity is endangering crop production Image: Burak Kara/Getty Images But as it declines, she and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels, and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals. Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worst with a drop of 85%, according to WWF's recent Living Planet report. It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature. "It is a really steep decline," said Shaw. "What it's telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it's an early warning indicator of the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unravelling." Deforestation directly drives biodiversity decline because forests are home to more than 80% of all land-based species Image: Juancho Torres/AA/picture alliance Thousands of policymakers, business leaders and civil society groups are meeting in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature loss by 2030. But progress towards those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges. What happens when ecosystem services decline or disappear? Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada's University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in Southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion (€2.63 billion) worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean. The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it. Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination. Why climate change is driving species loss To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a "pathway to collapse," warning that nature's decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability. "The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world," said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF's Living Planet report. "This is why we need to care about global biodiversity." It also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds. Poisonous frogs could be a source for new medications but as species disappear we could be missing out on novel drugs Image: Al Carrera/Zoonar/picture alliance Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds "inspired by nature," according to the World Health Organisation (WHO). As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments. Does it really matter if one species disappears? To return to the "nature as a team" metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute. But not always, particularly if it's a "keystone species." They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects. The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day. "No one would ever think, they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy," said Shaw. "But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume." People around the world rely on oysters and other marine life for their livelihoods and as a food source. Oysters are also a keystone species Image: Misper Apawu/AP Photo/picture alliance And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it "you lose the coastal protection." The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also impacts humans. Is humanity living through a sixth mass extinction and is it too late to prevent it? The planet has experienced five mass extinctions when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. Extinction is a natural process. But the rate at which species are disappearing today, suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event, driven largely by human activity, according to scientists. Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn't provoke despair. Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae says "the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm." And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover. The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture. Since sea otters on the North American Pacific Coast have rebounded, so too have kelp forests Image: Malcolm Schuyl/FLPA/imageBROKER/picture alliance Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests. That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection. Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover. "You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed," said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions. "We're learning how to turn things around at very small scales," said Shaw. "Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators." Baltic seagrass: restoring a secret climate ally To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Edited by: Tamsin Walker Advertisement

title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
body: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence Image source, POOL/AFP via Getty Images Image caption, President Emmanuel Macron urged calm in a national address following widespread looting and violence By Katya Adler Europe editor , Reporting from Paris Published 2 hours ago France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history. On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared. An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously. There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished. Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail. How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account? How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time? Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated? And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education? Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Vandals defaced Statue de la Republique in central Paris over the weekend On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France. He's apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Yet he and his interior minister are charged by many in France with being woefully ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests. The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened this weekend and why. "Things are dark in the city of light [a nickname for Paris]" was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night. Macron is widely viewed here as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There's a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines. That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets. Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks. Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets. What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment. People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation. Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility. "While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me. Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order,  posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented". For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday. But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests. France is holding its breath. Related topics Emmanuel Macron France French politics More on this story Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France Published 2 hours ago Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting Published 19 hours ago Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election? Published 3 days ago
retained_feed_body: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.

title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
body: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine Image source, Getty Images By Marc Ashdown , Business correspondent and Nick Edser , Business reporter Published 4 hours ago Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour. The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport. Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities. A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is also being launched. The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced. "We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000. The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said small changes in behaviour "can make a massive difference to people's experience on public transport". The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England. These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport Secretary Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100. The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will  deal with the incidents. Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyone The campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network". The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction". However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers". "Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said. Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with  different accessibility needs. He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police." Richard Holden MP, Shadow Transport Secretary, said: "After we led the charge against antisocial behaviour on public transport last summer, Ministers have worked out that nobody wants to endure pounding techno or blaring hip hop on a packed train or bus. "But passengers and railway staff face far more serious problems. Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways." Liberal Democrat Transport spokesperson, Olly Glover MP said: "Tough talk means nothing without enforcement. "Unless the Government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on." Independent watchdog Transport Focus said research it had published in June showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway. "Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell, Transport Focus's director of policy and insight. "Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport." Related topics Transport More on this story Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise Published 6 August Reported assaults on Britain's rail services rise by more than a third Published 24 September Safety concerns put Londoners off buses, say Tories Published 11 July

Antisocial behaviour on buses in England could lead to fines while a new campaign is also being launched for trains.
A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is being launched.

title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
body: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says Image source, Getty Images By Michael Race , Business reporter and Simon Jack , Business editor Published 28 minutes ago The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in". He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market. A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy. The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations. It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels. There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey. Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures. "Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia. "Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help. "I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union." The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%. The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years". "Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine. Image caption, Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer. But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment. All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently". At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added. Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began. Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids. "The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks." "Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged." Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history". "We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive." Related topics War in Ukraine Steel industry European Union Trade Ukraine International Business

title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
body: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured Image source, Getty Images By Jessica Murphy , Canada digital editor and Nadine Yousif , Senior Canada reporter , Reporting from Edmonton Published 50 minutes ago Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta. Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity". "The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died. Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening. Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC. Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing. "There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition. A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range. "What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he  said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area." Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there. News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation. Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable". The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said. In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference". What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base Published 2 hours ago Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright. The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down. Image source, EPA Image caption, Wainwright is about 200km (125 miles) from Edmonton, the provincial capital The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units. "It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province. STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed. Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance. Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said. "I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie". Additional reporting by Lisa Lambert Related topics Canada Alberta Military Mark Carney More on this story Several dead and injured in major fire at Canada military base Published 8 hours ago

title: 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight
body:
'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Close A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests on Saturday. Dramatic footage shared online shows the 19th-century building engulfed in flames, with the spire of its clock tower later collapsing. On Sunday, stunned residents watched as firefighters, who had battled the blaze through the night, assessed the building's structural integrity. Officials have not yet confirmed whether the town hall is at risk of collapse. "Damaging heritage buildings because you're angry with the government is selfish", one resident told the BBC. BBC correspondent Chris Bockman reports from Limoges. Read more about the protests across France. title: Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US
body:
Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US Close Warning: This video contains descriptions of drug-taking and distressing images A new wave of synthetic drugs is sweeping across the United States, raising fear of a worsening drug crisis. Earlier this year, President Donald Trump pledged a crackdown on drug cartels, proscribing many as terrorist organisations. Drug overdose deaths have fallen from a peak of around 110,000 in 2022, down to roughly 70,000 last year. However, America's decades-long drug crisis may be accelerating and authorities are increasingly concerned about cheaper, more powerful synthetic drugs, including an animal tranquilliser called tranq. The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from the frontlines in South Side, Chicago, where communities are battling the crisis. title: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France
body: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France Figure caption, Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of Paris By Jack Burgess Published 18 October 2026 Updated 2 hours ago French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday. In a national address from the Élysée Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame." Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted". Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry. The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings. Following some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history, France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will on Monday hold a crisis cabinet meeting . Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon. Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police. Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history. In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold. Image source, Mairie de Limoge Image caption, A view of the damage inside Limoges town hall on Sunday morning Speaking near the ruined building, Annèyse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody." "It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before." Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Fires were lit and shops looted during smaller scale disorder in Paris on Sunday Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas. Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings. The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations. Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A man tries to extinguish a fire in Paris on Sunday Student protests that began last month escalated significantly on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups. The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left. France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police. Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said. Jean-Luc Mélenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised Nuñez and police chiefs on social media. He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos". Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence". title: France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
body: Politics France France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists Andreas Noll 10/18/2026 October 18, 2026 Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left candidate win them over? https://p.dw.com/p/5OLUN Glucksmann has a difficult campaign ahead as the Socialist candidate Image: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance Advertisement The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11. Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election. As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI). The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate? Glucksmann was flour-bombed while leaving his victory celebration Image: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance Gluckmann's rapid rise "Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation. The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority. Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote. There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique. France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Melenchon's youth appeal Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen . France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left. The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention . At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France , he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education. In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under a lot of financial pressure. Four in ten households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200). Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35, and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens, or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise. Melenchon in Paris during a public sector strike on September 29 Image: Tom Nicholson/REUTERS Glucksmann's youth efforts The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election. Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron . France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement. The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car. Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon. This article was originally written in German. Advertisement

title: Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery
body:
Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery Close Pope Leo XIV held his first public engagement since his lung cancer surgery on Sunday, as he recited the Angelus prayer from the window of Vatican's Apostolic Palace. The surgery had taken place just a few days before, after Pope Leo had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. After the prayer, he thanked the people who have prayed for him in recent days and said he appreciated the support. He added he will now gradually return to his commitments as he recovers. Read more about the Pope's cancer diagnosis. title: Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops
body:
Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops Close Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence", as shopfronts were smashed and stores looted. For shop owners, this morning marks the start of clean-up efforts, with some reporting damages and stolen goods amount to €100,000 (£85,000). The BBC's James Waterhouse reports from the streets of Paris outside damaged buildings. Read more here. title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
body: Technology Ukraine How reliant is Ukraine on Starlink systems? Hannah Fuchs 10/18/2026 October 18, 2026 Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down? https://p.dw.com/p/5OMwD The Starlink satellite internet system has become a core component of Ukrainian defense Image: Adam88/Pond5 Images/IMAGO Advertisement Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink , central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk 's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use. How Starlink enables communications Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down. According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage. The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis , the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative. Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably. There are around 50,000 Starlink terminals in Ukraine Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications. This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX. The role of Starlink in drone warfare Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones . This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines. According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations. What throttling Starlink would mean According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph). Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind. Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities. More than just satellite internet However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them. This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory. The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units. This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States. Strategic dependence Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale. Starlink terminals enable mobile internet connection on the battlefield for the operation of drones Image: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies . Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare . Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition. This article has been translated from German. Advertisement

title: Turning the tides: Could hidden sea power energise our coastal towns?
body: Turning the tides: Could hidden sea power energise our coastal towns? Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, Engineer David Mummery says tidal power could change lives in coastal communities By Paul Hastie BBC Scotland Published 18 October 2026 In a secret location in the Highlands of Scotland, there's a fast-flowing river that's the key to understanding the massive power of water. It's where engineer David Mummery found himself more than a decade ago. With a length of cord tied tightly across the river, he swam out, gripped firmly, and let the unstoppable current rush over as he sunk his head below the surface. "As an engineer we do the maths and stuff," he says, "but sometimes you can get a lot more from actually touching the water and feeling it". As he lay down in the powerful rapids, he visualised a new type of small-scale tidal energy generator. It's an innovation he says could change lives for people in coastal communities. "I'd be under the river, feeling the turbulence of the water rushing over me. "Trying to envisage how this turbine needed to interact with that environment - to understand the way the water was working." Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, The Swimmer Turbine prototype at Strangford Narrows in Northern Ireland Mummery's idea became the Swimmer Turbine - a 50kw tidal generator named after his experience in the river. Anchored to the sea floor, the fiberglass and steel device lies invisible below the water's surface. It can generate enough electricity to power about 30 homes. He began tests in the river in early 2010s. On a patent lawyer's advice he found a secret location, far from curious Highland tourists and their cameras. "You're trying to be quite discreet because you're working with new technology," he says. It was in the first years of his company, Flex Marine Power, long before Britain was gripped by the soaring costs of an energy crisis. Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, Fishermen on Islay learn how to assemble the Swimmer Turbine The size of the Swimmer Turbine is what sets it apart from large tidal projects dotted around Scottish waters. Scotland is a world leader in the sector at sites including: Nova Innovation - The world's first tidal stream array, deployed in 2016 in Bluemull Sound in Shetland MeyGen - The world's largest tidal array, with four large 1.5MW turbines on the seabed of the Pentland Firth Orbital O2 -  The world's most powerful floating turbine, generating 2MW, anchored at Fall of Warness in the Orkney Islands Mummery's turbine is ultra compact and low cost compared to these giant machines. Fishermen and local workers can build and install it themselves from their own village harbour. "Can you imagine like an Ikea furniture kit? You get a shipping container and you'll open it up and it will be about 20 components. "You'll bolt them all together and then you've got your turbine ready. "There'll be a launch plan, you follow these instructions, then you'll be in the water." Mummery's work did not always focus on small-scale power. Originally from Guildford, he studied mechanical engineering at Surrey University. Before founding Flex Marine Power, he was a sought-after consultant in the UK energy sector. For a time he specialised in nuclear work and decommissioning, designing robots for pulling material out of contaminated tanks. He moved north after falling in love with a girl studying at Glasgow University. Jo became his wife and they now live in the city suburbs with three young children. Conveniently, Mummery's relocation came at a time when Scotland was establishing its reputation as a centre for marine power expertise. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The 180m-long Pelamis wave power project, nicknamed the sea snake In 2010 he took a secondment at Scottish Power Renewables on the ground-breaking Pelamis project in Orkney. The 180m-long (591ft) Pelamis P2 - nicknamed the sea snake - was the first deep-water, floating wave energy machine to generate power for the national grid. Ultimately, Pelamis went into administration in 2014 , but the ill-fated device remains celebrated as a milestone in marine power innovation. "The industry is littered with these examples of fantastic technologies and teams that do brave things that take decades," Mummery says. "But at some point the market doesn't step up and they falter. Some really good ones have lasted the course, but others have not and it's sad." Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, David Mummery at home in Glasgow, where he established Flex Marine Power Mummery says the UK has "phenomenal waters for tidal power" and he loved being a part of major projects - but couldn't shake a discomfort. His work felt incongruous to the many small coastal communities he found himself in. "I'd be going out on boats around Scotland doing sonar surveys with all these really expensive pieces of kit. "But the equipment was all really big, utility-scale stuff that would weigh hundreds of tonnes, shipped by people from the mainland. "All the people I was meeting in harbours or in the pub were fishermen. And they were knowledgeable and they were interested. "I thought 'we've got to do this in a way that they can take the lead'." That, he says, is what motivated his Swimmer Turbine idea. Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, The Swimmer Turbine is assembled on land and can be launched from a slipway In 2011 he left big projects behind to found Flex Marine Power and focus on his turbine concept. He spent hours at his desk sketching, working out how to make the technology smaller and lighter. He hired a student employee and found a sleek, glass office space outside Glasgow - which he quickly discovered wasn't entirely suited to an engineer and his tools. "It was a lovely place, but I wasn't allowed to take a hammer drill into the office. "We were trying to make prototype turbines under the desk so the landlord wouldn't see them when he came in." Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, Learning the ropes, the local team in training off the coast of Islay Mummery turned to Clydeside's shipbuilding past in search of a more suitable workspace. He presented a plan to convert former shipyards for marine technology research, and was invited to Greenock by Inverclyde's redevelopment authority. "There were lots of empty sheds that hadn't been used for years," he says. "They basically said 'we'll walk you around, you can pick a shed'. So I got the pick of the bunch right on the quayside." Mummery now had direct access to the River Clyde for sea trials to test his models. He developed a prototype which he successfully trialled in 2015 on the island of Luing, in the Firth of Lorn, near Oban. It secured Flex Marine's first major investment and expansion the following year. Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, The Swimmer turbine can be installed without large cranes or heavy lift equipment The next major step was in Northern Ireland in 2020, at Strangford Narrows in County Down. Mummery worked with Queen's University Belfast who had an academic license to test tidal equipment at sea. "Me and Mark, my accountant, lifted all of the components into a shipping container and sent it out on a lorry. "We were introduced to a bunch of local mariners. We pulled off a full-scale tidal turbine installation out of a container deposited in a farmyard." Generating electricity while tethered to the back of a boat, Mummery says it was the full-scale proof-of-concept that "finally put us on the map". It helped Flex Marine Power secure £968,000 from the UK government's Energy Entrepreneurs Fund for a team of nine people to develop a commercial turbine model. This version would not be tied to a boat. The Swimmer Turbine would launch directly from shore and remain absolutely hidden, generating electricity below the surface of the water. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The waters of Islay are perfect for whisky and the tidal energy industry Mummery took it through months of testing last year on the island of Islay - famous for its many whisky distilleries and coastal waters that are perfect for tidal power. He rented space at a boatyard where "talented local people" were taught how to assemble and launch the device. Finally, after his years of work, came the defining moment. "I was standing at the end of the slipway, seeing our machine, without any of my guys touching it. "It was all local people. Fishermen, using their own tractor, launching it down their own slipway. This was my vision in a nutshell." Image source, Flex Marine Power Image caption, Assembled from a shipping container, the turbine is invisible below the water surface The next stage is putting the power to good use. Mummery will return to Islay next year with a plan to generate electricity for the island. "The sea is a very big space and these things are invisible. There could be different tidal arrays in different parts of the island, all owned by different people. "In those real coastal communities, they don't have flashy cranes and heavy lifting capabilities and big corporate companies with big pockets. "But what they do have is knowledge and work ethic and a deep understanding of their environment and the sea. "We're trying to equip real people to thrive by giving them access to the power that's in the tides." Related topics Scotland Renewable energy Energy industry Isle of Islay Wave tech 'belongs in a museum not a scrapyard' Published 4 August 2023 'Most powerful' tidal-powered turbine switched on Published 28 July 2021 Shetland tidal array to be extended Published 6 July 2017 More on this story Flex Marine Power

title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
body: Politics Czech Republic Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections Timothy Jones Reuters, dpa, AP 10/18/2026 October 18, 2026 Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition. https://p.dw.com/p/5ONFe Babis has been described as 'Trumpist' in his outlook Image: Beata Zawrzel/ZUMA/IMAGO Advertisement The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate . The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament. The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier. What happened in the Czech Senate elections? Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority. The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers. Babis called the result "catastrophic." "We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda. That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters. Czech journalists warn of dangers of public media reform To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming. Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges. title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
body: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies Image source, Reuters By Max Matza Published 17 October 2026 Updated 18 October 2026 Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens. The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September. But Trump issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions. Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Trump's order was "an important and truly historic moment", and that the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market. Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support. Since then, Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin. The sanctions suspension seemed to add further fuel to the fire. Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end". He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter." Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground. Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network Published 2 days ago Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC Published 2 days ago The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India. It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the suspension would consist of a 60-day pause to allow for the Trump administration to analyse the impact they might have on the US and global economy. The suspension drew criticism from US politicians from both main parties. Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky. A handful of Republicans also came out against the move. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Trump ally, called waiving the sanctions a mistake, telling Fox News that there were other ways to address fuel prices, while the state's other Senatory John Cornyn called the move "reckless". North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible", arguing that Trump could bring energy prices down by ending the Iran war instead of "doing a solid" for Putin. Nebraska Representative Don Bacon indicated that US lawmakers will now resist funding Trump's agenda. Figure caption, Watch: Will Ukraine get the support needed as tensions with US rise? Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. He told reporters on Saturday that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia. Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies initially criticised Trump for his plans to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of rising fuel costs ahead of the US midterm elections, with inflation souring his standing with the American public. Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Zelensky expressed surprise at the announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days of fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries. Trump condemned the Ukrainian strikes as a disgrace, but Zelensky said he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Zaporizhzhia was among regions hit by Russian strikes overnight Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. Last week, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues. However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds. Trump has denied deliberately slowing down the network and denied another accusation by Zelensky that US had withdrawn intelligence-sharing. Ukrainian authorities said that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country since Friday. That included an ambulance driver killed and 20 others injured in a Russian strike on the city of Kherson, they said. Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan and Sareen Habeshian Related topics War in Ukraine Russia sanctions Donald Trump Russia More on this story Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace' Published 2 days ago Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia Published 7 days ago Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill Published 18 September Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume Published 3 days ago
